title: Should robots make decisions for people?
summary: Look back at what your trained model got wrong, steelman the other side, then debate whether robots should be allowed to make decisions for people.

steps.title: Evidence from the model you trained
steps.body:
A few weeks ago you trained a model in Teachable Machine to recognize three hand signs, then tested it on situations it had never been trained on: your other hand, a darker room, someone else's hand, a sign held far back or only half in the frame. Some of those probably tripped it up, even though the model looked like it worked great in the easy cases.

That mattered even though it was only a hand sign. Now think bigger: what if a machine like that one day decides something real about a person, whether someone gets a loan, whether an answer on a test counts as correct, whether a security camera flags someone as suspicious? A model that only knows what it was shown can be wrong in exactly the same way your hand-sign model was wrong, except the mistake now lands on a real person instead of a wrong guess on a screen.

Steelman first, same rule as every debate this season: before you argue your own side, say the strongest version of the other side's point, in your own words, not a weak one. Someone arguing robots should decide might say a machine never gets tired, never plays favorites, and can look through more information than a person ever could in the time it has. Someone arguing robots should not decide might say a machine only knows what it was shown, cannot explain a decision the way a person can be asked to, and cannot be reasoned with the way a person can.

Back up every point with claim, reason, example, same as before. This week's second skill is cross-examination: after the other side makes a point, ask one real question that tests it, not just a comment. A cross-examination question digs at exactly what would have to be true for their point to hold up, the same way you asked what the model would have needed to see in training to get a hard case right.

Three rounds, and the motion is the question itself: robots should be allowed to make decisions for people.

steps.title: Record it
steps.prompt: Record part of the debate, or record yourself afterward explaining one thing your trained model got wrong and how that connects to a machine deciding something for a real person.
